Perform a holistic reading of the following transcript. Identify "meaning units" that capture phrases, moments, and expressions central to the participant's lived experience of marching arts membership.
Provide output as a JSON object with a key 'meaning_units' which is a list of strings.
Transcript:
My time in marching band taught me a lot about life in many different ways. Tangible things it taught me were things like leadership, responsibility, relationship building, getting a little more detailed time management, how to be a problem solver, how to use a forethought and think ahead and try to avoid problems before they even happened. It taught me how to be a leader, how to work well with my peers. I was section leader for one year in high school, drum major for two years in high school, and then section leader again for three years in college, and just how to work with all different types of people as a skill that really benefits me in my job now in adulthood. More of the intangible things I guess would be just building relationships with people. I'm having a group of friends or maybe not even friends but a group of people that I knew would have my back just because I was a part of their organization. Best memories I have from band are anything I did with my friends in high school, going out to eat after football games together, voting to band kids into homecoming king and queen my senior year. What else? I don't know those were just those were just my people, the people I looked for in the hallways, looked for in every class. And then in college it was the same thing but it was people who 100% chose to be there and as goofy and as silly as we were, we all knew deep down that we all chose to be there, to be a part of something bigger than us, make music together, to be good. And knowing that people were counting on you to do your part and that you were also counting on them to do theirs kind of just had this underlying you know bond with people. Let's see... What marching arts gave you? I mean if you want to go like super big picture really marching band led me to who I am today in literally every sense of my life. I met my husband in marching band at University of Houston but I decided to go to the University of Houston because my high school band director went there and he told me if I want to do music education then that's where I should go. So I listened to him and I went and kind of something that's a really cool moment for me is both of my high school directors were associated with University of Houston where I ended up going to college and little did I know that there was a lot of people at University of Houston that are associated with where I went to school, Birdville High School, Birdville ISD. Mr. Green had come out to my high school multiple times. I had no idea he was affiliated with the University of Houston until I got to rehearsal and boom there he was. Mr. Burtman of course taught in the district. One of my college band directors taught in the district I came from so we had a ton of mutual contacts, mutual people that we both knew. So learning all the ties that my university band program had to my high school band program just made it even that more meaningful. I met my best friend freshman year in college band. We both were in the same section, in the same marching band, in the same ensembles with each other and we were roommates all through college and our kids know each other so that's one of my favorite relationships. I'll never forget my first year in college marching band how I was still in like high school marching band mode of like standing at attention and set and check and all of those commands and I look over and some of the upperclassmen were like had their phones out and I was just shocked. I was like we're allowed to have our phones out at rehearsal and then like the first football game we were in uniform up in the stands and they were passing out like sodas and cans of coke and I'm like we can drink soda in our uniforms because that was not the case when I was in high school. So going from high school band you know strict rules every procedure has to be followed to a tee to college marching band where it's like you're responsible for yourself you know do the right thing or don't but that was that was a bit of shock for me as a freshman coming into college marching band. Another one of my favorite memories is getting the flute section to have the flutes in the front campaign in college. We were always you know up at the top of the stands nobody really cared we're always in the back of the marching field nobody really cared so we would just start campaigning for ourselves to be at the front any chance we could get and that we had a lot we had some good times uh cracking jokes and doing things that people didn't know we were doing because we were being bitter and being petty about always being put in the back. I think that's it for now Go Cougs!

    "Band friendship as everyday ritual and memory: “going out to eat after football games together.”",
    "Collective identity and recognition: “voting band kids into homecoming king and queen my senior year.”",
    "College band intensifying commitment: people who “100% chose to be there… to be a part of something bigger than us.”",
    "Shared purpose as a bond: “make music together, to be good.”",
    "Mutual dependence as an “underlying… bond”: “people were counting on you to do your part and… you were also counting on them.”",

    "Meeting a life partner through membership: “I met my husband in marching band at University of Houston.”",
    "Following a director’s guidance as a pivotal path: choosing UH because a trusted mentor said “that’s where I should go… So I listened to him.”",
    "Discovering an unexpected web of connections between programs: “learning all the ties… just made it even that more meaningful.”",
    "A “cool moment” of recognition and continuity: arriving at rehearsal and realizing “boom there he was” (a familiar figure now at the university).",
    "Band producing enduring, family-level friendship: “I met my best friend… we were roommates all through college and our kids know each other.”",
    "Feeling ‘out of place’ at first in college band: being in “high school marching band mode” of strict commands and “standing at attention.”",
    "Freshman “shock” at a new culture of autonomy: upperclassmen “had their phones out,” and realizing “we’re allowed” to do that at rehearsal.",
    "Another shock of relaxed norms: “we can drink soda in our uniforms,” contrasting with high school’s stricter expectations.",
    "A key shift in responsibility: from “strict rules every procedure… to a tee” to “you’re responsible for yourself… do the right thing or don’t.”",
    "Pride and agency through advocacy: “getting the flute section to have the flutes in the front… start campaigning for ourselves.”",
    "Experiencing marginalization in placement: “always… at the top of the stands… always in the back… nobody really cared.”",
    "Using humor and ‘petty’ solidarity to cope and resist: “cracking jokes… doing things that people didn’t know… being bitter and being petty.”",
    "Closing with continued identification and allegiance: “Go Cougs!”"
  ]
}

Given the transcript and meaning units, perform interpretive thematizing and whole-part reconciliation. Develop these into textural and structural descriptions reflecting core dimensions of experience.
Output as a JSON object with a key 'themes' containing a list of objects (with 'theme_name' and 'description').

Transcript:
Hello, my name is Reid Beicher and I marched the Cavaliers from 2022 to 2025 on baritone. My first core experience and memory with the Cavaliers was my first year during spring training. I was an 18-year-old who just turned 18. I was contracted as a 17-year-old still in high school and so I had never really experienced anything beyond a high school band in Cypress, Texas named Langham Creek High School with very many prestigious years and directors and all these things. But at the time that I went to that school we started to get smaller and the experience was, while incredibly amazing, was not what it was before my time. And don't get me wrong, it was still incredible, just not what it was. It was a different set of kids, it's a different culture. The school was getting smaller, our demographics were changing, the culture was different than it was 10 years before that. So going into this group that was very different than anything I've experienced. The most brass members I had ever marched was 49 other brass members my freshman year of high school. So incredibly different environment, different everything. And I remember going in to spring training and arriving a week late and having to learn drill. And I remember I had learned the drill the week of back home and I remember trying to get on the field and me getting very frustrated about how I was doing. To the point that I started to like cry beneath my sunglasses because I was just so frustrated that I was not picking it up as quickly as the people that had been here a week had. And it was a very frustrating experience and I remember later that night or that week sitting in a room with a group of guys who I really didn't know but they were mostly veteran members and I remember telling them about how frustrated I was and how I started to cry and all these emotions right. I was very, like I said at Langham it was a very different program than anything I had experienced from drum corps to Langham. And I was used to being one of the better marchers, one of the better players on the field at all times. And going to this environment where I was being pushed and what I was giving wasn't good enough and all this was something that hit me very emotionally. I remember sitting in this room with this group of guys and they started to hear how I was talking about my experiences and how then they decided to take it amongst themselves to start telling their own experiences and times that they've gotten frustrated and cried and felt like they were less than worthy and that comfort, that shared experience which is a huge word I will always go back to later in this. The word shared experience was something that connected me so closely with these people that I didn't know were my brothers yet but they were my brothers. And that made me feel loved and seen like they know what I've been through even though they don't. They don't know exactly how I feel but I feel like they did. That was very special. Throughout the course of my rookie year we hit a massive roadblock. We got COVID and I don't believe we rehearsed as a full corps for 21 straight days. Understandably that led to a lot of frustrations amongst the membership, a lot of pointing fingers, a lot of this and that, bets, blaming new guys, all of that. It was very toxic. By the end of the year, frankly, we hated each other. It was awful. I remember going back into my environment, my people, my family. I remember leaving the banquet, getting into the Uber and the first thing I said to my family was, I never want to march the Cavaliers ever again because it was so miserable by the end that I wanted nothing to do with the Corps. And it's not like I didn't have my fair share of bad experiences. My senior year at Langham Creek was the first time that we missed area finals in marching band for a long time and I was the brass captain of that group. I felt a lot of that on myself and it was a very inexperienced, a very raw group of players and I felt a lot of that pressure on myself that maybe I didn't do my part as well or I could have done more. And looking back, I could have only controlled so much, really. That experience towards the end of the season, how we treat each other, said a lot about what we ended up feeling as a group. I think that when we were all happy and had high expectations for the season upcoming during spring training, we all got along better. That shared experience was different. As soon as people started coming at each other's throats and all of these things, that experience changed. I remember after that off-season, getting really close to another Cavalier and UH alum, his name is Hunter Dorman. He teaches at Grand Oaks High School now. I remember him talking about the 2015 Cavalier season, which they got 9th place that year. There was a massive sickness. It wasn't a good time. Very similar to 2022, right? And he talked about it and there's this quote I'll never forget, was said by Hunter Doogie, their drum major at the time. I didn't know we were doing bad until someone told me we were. And that really hit heavy with me because I remember a lot my rookie year that we had hyped ourselves up to be like, this is going to be great. The staff was telling us we're great. All this leading through the off-season and spring training, this is going to be amazing. We're going to medal, all this stuff, all this stuff. And we laid egg at the first show because we frankly weren't that good. Everyone outside of the sphere could see that, outside of our bubble could see that. And from there, the demeanor of the staff and the core changed. They're like, are we bad? That attitude shift, worrying about something that wasn't our own work, but rather what someone thought of our work, put each other against, we started pitting each other against each other. And a very similar thing happened my third year in the core. The second year was good. It was good. It was a step in the right direction, competitively. It wasn't where we wanted it to be, but it was sure better than ninth place. We got eighth place, right? One better, who cares? I don't care about the score, but culture-wise, it was a much more positive, hardworking group of people. And we were awful, but we worked hard. So we enter the third year and we have some pretty high expectations, but going into these off-season camps, it was rough. We had lost a lot of older members the previous year, because there was a lot of age outs that came from the Blue Knights because of staff changes that happened. A lot of the Blue Knights staff moved to the Cavaliers in 2023. And with them, a lot of older members who all aged out or all realized that the Cavaliers was a very different drum corps than the Blue Knights. In the Cavaliers, we focused and prioritized more on fraternization, shared experience, brotherhood. For a lot of those Blue Knights people, they're just looking to have a good drum corps experience, and that was about it. But my third year, we started okay competitively. And like I talked about earlier, it's an okay experience because we're focused on what we do, and that's about it. And then we start getting beat by corps that we don't think we should be getting beat by, which ultimately doesn't matter. We're still getting beat by them. You can say all you want, but at the end of the day, even if we look at ourselves, we aren't holding up what we needed to do. And I remember that turned out into an all-out crazy fest. The brass was pitting against the percussion and this and that, and we were just all fighting. And as a third year, I'm part of the veteran leadership. Not leadership as in like instated leadership of the group, but the veterans, the older veterans. And I remember there was one night where our horn sergeant, which this goes beyond anything that is acceptable in any sense or form, this is not okay. We were in West Virginia, I believe, some state over there, and we had been not doing good competitively. So our horn sergeant made an emotional decision to show that if we don't hold up our end of the bargain, if one person, one gear doesn't work and do their job, it all comes falling down. And so we, and the Cavaliers, we would always shine our shoes. And a couple of people were infamous for not shining their shoes, doing what's expected of them, their part, just like they would do in the show. And so our horn sergeant that year decided that he wanted the proof of point by making, by having every single brass horn line member get their shoes after rehearsal and put them on the ground. And line up. Now if you know anything about hazing, lines are usually not good, not a good sign. And the JOs, the junior officers, so we're talking about the drum majors and the horn sergeant and then some section leaders, went down the line and looking at every single pair of shoes. And they pulled out the shoes that didn't look good, didn't look like they had been polished and they pulled those shoes out and they had those people come out. And then they told those people that they would shine their shoes. And they would shine their shoes while each, every other horn line member would run, run laps around them in a parking lot in the middle of nowhere at 11 p.m. at night after a full day of rehearsal when everyone else is going to sleep. This wasn't acceptable, wasn't acceptable by any means. And we ran. And what that turned into was one of the worst things ever. It pitted our members and our horn line against each other. We had enemies. We had people to blame. You're holding us back. You're the reason why we're getting 11th place. You're the reason why we're losing to the Colts and the Troopers and the whatevers. And that was, that shared, because we didn't have a shared experience, because we weren't all in it together, because we were fighting against each other, that tore apart the group. Because we didn't have a shared positive experience. And for the Cavaliers, we pride ourselves on brotherhood. I am able to meet a brother and know a brother and know that they have a shared experience, an experience that is very similar to mine. They know how, what I've gone through. And because of that, I love them, even though I don't know them. And of course, you know, that's all bandy band stuff. And at some point, you know, that experience for some, for me, especially my last year went really great until the very end, which was bittersweet. The end was just kind of ruined by some personal life stuff, not anything having to really do with what was going on inside the Corps. And that was rough. For me, marching band is everything. Drum Corps is everything, because of the shared experience. And if it is either a negative shared experience, or an experience that pits us against each other, even though we're a team, that will create a lot of animosity and bad experiences. The great thing about Langham was that there was a family there. We may have not been doing, we were going through a lot of transitions, and not in a bad way, it was just different. Mr. Maris had just retired. Just when the culture of the band, you know, it was, it was different than when she started. It was a different group of kids. We were nearing, we had just gotten hit by the pandemic, numbers were low, all this stuff. And when Mr. Thomas, who did an awesome job, was handed the keys after COVID, it was different. Not in a bad way, in a different way. But for us, what kept a lot of us together, even though we were upset, and the reason why I had a positive experience, I would say, the last couple of years of my time at Langham, even though competitively, we didn't do that great, and we were upset by it, was because of the people. I loved those kids dearly when I was a senior, and I would do anything for them. And I treated them like my family, better than my family, I would say. And that experience was something that I sometimes got at the Cavaliers. I had an okay experience with the Cavaliers in four years, and I stayed there a long time because I believed that we could make a change and help, and we did. By my last year, we had made a positive change in the brotherhood, in the culture of the group, but man, it took three years to get there. Three really rough years. The second was okay, but the first and third year were really rough. But by 2025, the group had mostly changed. We were mostly on the same page together. Granted, yeah, there was internal stuff between the junior officers and specifically the drum majors and the membership and the veterans against the drum majors, and that was just messy. That was a couple of people not really holding up their part, but everyone else was still in it. The staff, my last year, most of them were Cavaliers, and that was really special and contributed in a way to bring us together. They had a shared experience that was positive, that the Cavaliers had changed their life for the better, just like myself. And because of that, I was able to connect with them, and I felt loved and cared about them. One of my dear mentors, I don't know if I can even say mentor, because I don't talk to him as much as I probably should, but I loved him dearly, is Jeremy Sinica. Like I said, the end of my last year was rough, and I remember the day that it happened, Jeremy had talked to me almost half of the visual block while I was crying, just sobbing for him. And he was with me, and he cared and loved me and did anything. And even after the season, checking up on me, talking to me, all these things, and I'll never forget him, because of he understands, because of a shared experience that he had similar to mine. I think that's such an important part of marching band is, and drum corps, the shared experience. Shared experience is everything. It can be great, it can be bad, but when there isn't a shared experience, that's not good.

Transcript:
Hello, my name is Reid Beicher and I marched the Cavaliers from 2022 to 2025 on baritone. My first core experience and memory with the Cavaliers was my first year during spring training. I was an 18-year-old who just turned 18. I was contracted as a 17-year-old still in high school and so I had never really experienced anything beyond a high school band in Cypress, Texas named Langham Creek High School with very many prestigious years and directors and all these things. But at the time that I went to that school we started to get smaller and the experience was, while incredibly amazing, was not what it was before my time. And don't get me wrong, it was still incredible, just not what it was. It was a different set of kids, it's a different culture. The school was getting smaller, our demographics were changing, the culture was different than it was 10 years before that. So going into this group that was very different than anything I've experienced. The most brass members I had ever marched was 49 other brass members my freshman year of high school. So incredibly different environment, different everything. And I remember going in to spring training and arriving a week late and having to learn drill. And I remember I had learned the drill the week of back home and I remember trying to get on the field and me getting very frustrated about how I was doing. To the point that I started to like cry beneath my sunglasses because I was just so frustrated that I was not picking it up as quickly as the people that had been here a week had. And it was a very frustrating experience and I remember later that night or that week sitting in a room with a group of guys who I really didn't know but they were mostly veteran members and I remember telling them about how frustrated I was and how I started to cry and all these emotions right. I was very, like I said at Langham it was a very different program than anything I had experienced from drum corps to Langham. And I was used to being one of the better marchers, one of the better players on the field at all times. And going to this environment where I was being pushed and what I was giving wasn't good enough and all this was something that hit me very emotionally. I remember sitting in this room with this group of guys and they started to hear how I was talking about my experiences and how then they decided to take it amongst themselves to start telling their own experiences and times that they've gotten frustrated and cried and felt like they were less than worthy and that comfort, that shared experience which is a huge word I will always go back to later in this. The word shared experience was something that connected me so closely with these people that I didn't know were my brothers yet but they were my brothers. And that made me feel loved and seen like they know what I've been through even though they don't. They don't know exactly how I feel but I feel like they did. That was very special. Throughout the course of my rookie year we hit a massive roadblock. We got COVID and I don't believe we rehearsed as a full corps for 21 straight days. Understandably that led to a lot of frustrations amongst the membership, a lot of pointing fingers, a lot of this and that, bets, blaming new guys, all of that. It was very toxic. By the end of the year, frankly, we hated each other. It was awful. I remember going back into my environment, my people, my family. I remember leaving the banquet, getting into the Uber and the first thing I said to my family was, I never want to march the Cavaliers ever again because it was so miserable by the end that I wanted nothing to do with the Corps. And it's not like I didn't have my fair share of bad experiences. My senior year at Langham Creek was the first time that we missed area finals in marching band for a long time and I was the brass captain of that group. I felt a lot of that on myself and it was a very inexperienced, a very raw group of players and I felt a lot of that pressure on myself that maybe I didn't do my part as well or I could have done more. And looking back, I could have only controlled so much, really. That experience towards the end of the season, how we treat each other, said a lot about what we ended up feeling as a group. I think that when we were all happy and had high expectations for the season upcoming during spring training, we all got along better. That shared experience was different. As soon as people started coming at each other's throats and all of these things, that experience changed. I remember after that off-season, getting really close to another Cavalier and UH alum, his name is Hunter Dorman. He teaches at Grand Oaks High School now. I remember him talking about the 2015 Cavalier season, which they got 9th place that year. There was a massive sickness. It wasn't a good time. Very similar to 2022, right? And he talked about it and there's this quote I'll never forget, was said by Hunter Doogie, their drum major at the time. I didn't know we were doing bad until someone told me we were. And that really hit heavy with me because I remember a lot my rookie year that we had hyped ourselves up to be like, this is going to be great. The staff was telling us we're great. All this leading through the off-season and spring training, this is going to be amazing. We're going to medal, all this stuff, all this stuff. And we laid egg at the first show because we frankly weren't that good. Everyone outside of the sphere could see that, outside of our bubble could see that. And from there, the demeanor of the staff and the core changed. They're like, are we bad? That attitude shift, worrying about something that wasn't our own work, but rather what someone thought of our work, put each other against, we started pitting each other against each other. And a very similar thing happened my third year in the core. The second year was good. It was good. It was a step in the right direction, competitively. It wasn't where we wanted it to be, but it was sure better than ninth place. We got eighth place, right? One better, who cares? I don't care about the score, but culture-wise, it was a much more positive, hardworking group of people. And we were awful, but we worked hard. So we enter the third year and we have some pretty high expectations, but going into these off-season camps, it was rough. We had lost a lot of older members the previous year, because there was a lot of age outs that came from the Blue Knights because of staff changes that happened. A lot of the Blue Knights staff moved to the Cavaliers in 2023. And with them, a lot of older members who all aged out or all realized that the Cavaliers was a very different drum corps than the Blue Knights. In the Cavaliers, we focused and prioritized more on fraternization, shared experience, brotherhood. For a lot of those Blue Knights people, they're just looking to have a good drum corps experience, and that was about it. But my third year, we started okay competitively. And like I talked about earlier, it's an okay experience because we're focused on what we do, and that's about it. And then we start getting beat by corps that we don't think we should be getting beat by, which ultimately doesn't matter. We're still getting beat by them. You can say all you want, but at the end of the day, even if we look at ourselves, we aren't holding up what we needed to do. And I remember that turned out into an all-out crazy fest. The brass was pitting against the percussion and this and that, and we were just all fighting. And as a third year, I'm part of the veteran leadership. Not leadership as in like instated leadership of the group, but the veterans, the older veterans. And I remember there was one night where our horn sergeant, which this goes beyond anything that is acceptable in any sense or form, this is not okay. We were in West Virginia, I believe, some state over there, and we had been not doing good competitively. So our horn sergeant made an emotional decision to show that if we don't hold up our end of the bargain, if one person, one gear doesn't work and do their job, it all comes falling down. And so we, and the Cavaliers, we would always shine our shoes. And a couple of people were infamous for not shining their shoes, doing what's expected of them, their part, just like they would do in the show. And so our horn sergeant that year decided that he wanted the proof of point by making, by having every single brass horn line member get their shoes after rehearsal and put them on the ground. And line up. Now if you know anything about hazing, lines are usually not good, not a good sign. And the JOs, the junior officers, so we're talking about the drum majors and the horn sergeant and then some section leaders, went down the line and looking at every single pair of shoes. And they pulled out the shoes that didn't look good, didn't look like they had been polished and they pulled those shoes out and they had those people come out. And then they told those people that they would shine their shoes. And they would shine their shoes while each, every other horn line member would run, run laps around them in a parking lot in the middle of nowhere at 11 p.m. at night after a full day of rehearsal when everyone else is going to sleep. This wasn't acceptable, wasn't acceptable by any means. And we ran. And what that turned into was one of the worst things ever. It pitted our members and our horn line against each other. We had enemies. We had people to blame. You're holding us back. You're the reason why we're getting 11th place. You're the reason why we're losing to the Colts and the Troopers and the whatevers. And that was, that shared, because we didn't have a shared experience, because we weren't all in it together, because we were fighting against each other, that tore apart the group. Because we didn't have a shared positive experience. And for the Cavaliers, we pride ourselves on brotherhood. I am able to meet a brother and know a brother and know that they have a shared experience, an experience that is very similar to mine. They know how, what I've gone through. And because of that, I love them, even though I don't know them. And of course, you know, that's all bandy band stuff. And at some point, you know, that experience for some, for me, especially my last year went really great until the very end, which was bittersweet. The end was just kind of ruined by some personal life stuff, not anything having to really do with what was going on inside the Corps. And that was rough. For me, marching band is everything. Drum Corps is everything, because of the shared experience. And if it is either a negative shared experience, or an experience that pits us against each other, even though we're a team, that will create a lot of animosity and bad experiences. The great thing about Langham was that there was a family there. We may have not been doing, we were going through a lot of transitions, and not in a bad way, it was just different. Mr. Maris had just retired. Just when the culture of the band, you know, it was, it was different than when she started. It was a different group of kids. We were nearing, we had just gotten hit by the pandemic, numbers were low, all this stuff. And when Mr. Thomas, who did an awesome job, was handed the keys after COVID, it was different. Not in a bad way, in a different way. But for us, what kept a lot of us together, even though we were upset, and the reason why I had a positive experience, I would say, the last couple of years of my time at Langham, even though competitively, we didn't do that great, and we were upset by it, was because of the people. I loved those kids dearly when I was a senior, and I would do anything for them. And I treated them like my family, better than my family, I would say. And that experience was something that I sometimes got at the Cavaliers. I had an okay experience with the Cavaliers in four years, and I stayed there a long time because I believed that we could make a change and help, and we did. By my last year, we had made a positive change in the brotherhood, in the culture of the group, but man, it took three years to get there. Three really rough years. The second was okay, but the first and third year were really rough. But by 2025, the group had mostly changed. We were mostly on the same page together. Granted, yeah, there was internal stuff between the junior officers and specifically the drum majors and the membership and the veterans against the drum majors, and that was just messy. That was a couple of people not really holding up their part, but everyone else was still in it. The staff, my last year, most of them were Cavaliers, and that was really special and contributed in a way to bring us together. They had a shared experience that was positive, that the Cavaliers had changed their life for the better, just like myself. And because of that, I was able to connect with them, and I felt loved and cared about them. One of my dear mentors, I don't know if I can even say mentor, because I don't talk to him as much as I probably should, but I loved him dearly, is Jeremy Sinica. Like I said, the end of my last year was rough, and I remember the day that it happened, Jeremy had talked to me almost half of the visual block while I was crying, just sobbing for him. And he was with me, and he cared and loved me and did anything. And even after the season, checking up on me, talking to me, all these things, and I'll never forget him, because of he understands, because of a shared experience that he had similar to mine. I think that's such an important part of marching band is, and drum corps, the shared experience. Shared experience is everything. It can be great, it can be bad, but when there isn't a shared experience, that's not good.
